entries.title: Emperor of Nothing by Blake J Harris review – the definitive portrait of Larry David
entries.summary: The Seinfeld creator went from luckless standup to multi-millionaire – but what’s his secret? Larry David agreed to this authorised biography with a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.” As Blake J Harris tells it, the comedy writer has always been adept at finding reasons not to do something, or to stop doing it, even when there’s nothing to fall back on. As a peppery standup in 1970s New York
entries.content:
Larry David agreed to this authorised biography with a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.” As Blake J Harris tells it, the comedy writer has always been adept at finding reasons not to do something, or to stop doing it, even when there’s nothing to fall back on. As a peppery standup in 1970s New York, David was notorious for storming off stage if the audience displeased him. He walked out of his first TV job, on the Saturday Night Live clone Fridays, because “I stunk.” He twice quit Seinfeld, the sitcom he co-created in 1989, over meddling by NBC executives and fantasised about the network giving him an excuse to leave for good. In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, he told friends, “Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.” He was only half joking.

David’s career proves that it is in fact possible to be immensely, groundbreakingly successful without ever displaying great ambition. Growing up in Brooklyn amid a boisterous extended family, Lawrence Gene David loved baseball and tall tales but, oddly, not making people laugh. “I can’t recall him ever saying a funny thing,” remembers his older brother Ken. After a spell in the army reserve, he drifted through low-effort jobs – limo driver, bra salesman – and dropped out of acting school, partly because his classmate Jeff Goldblum showed him what a real actor looked like. “Most of the time I was just waiting for other people to stop talking so that I could start talking,” he admits.

Hence standup. In 1977, Variety magazine summed up David’s themes as “sexual fantasies, oriental yodeling, baldness, hypochondria, growing up with Jewish parents, college, porno movies, etc”. Much as they admired his integrity, his peers considered him too self-destructive and uncompromising to make it. One contemporary says that if you had polled New York’s standups, “Larry would have been voted Least Likely to Ever Accomplish Anything. Including by Larry himself!” After a few unhappy forays into television, David was already 41 when he began writing a pilot with the amiable, ultra-professional Jerry Seinfeld.

Authorised biographies tend to flatter their subjects, but then there doesn’t seem to be much dirt to dig. Compared with Harris’s last subject, the obnoxious virtual reality entrepreneur Palmer Luckey, David is a pretty solid guy who still has the close friends he made 50 years ago. There is no evidence here of those familiar funnyman archetypes, the sad clown and the secret monster. Harris was therefore able to access every important figure in his life, including fellow comedian Richard Lewis, his best friend, and Rob Reiner, whose company produced Seinfeld, before they died. Augmented by transcripts and memos, the quotes are so plentiful that the book often feels more like an oral history than a conventional biography, especially the Seinfeld section. If you want to read multi-page breakdowns of classic episodes like The Soup Nazi and The Chinese Restaurant (I do), then you’re in luck.

In the self-referential fourth season, Jerry pitches a sitcom, starring himself, that is “about nothing”. Seinfeld itself was never that but it was the first show to root itself in everyday conversations, altercations and humiliations, many of which David had been recording in notebooks for years. One of the pleasures of this book is encountering a funny incident in the 70s that resurfaces on screen 20 years later. “There are people in this world that funny things happen to,” says Seinfeld. “And he is one of them.” Jason Alexander once complained to David that his character George Costanza had an implausible storyline: nobody would behave like this in real life. “What are you talking about?” David replied. “This happened to me, and this is exactly what I did.”

Making Seinfeld was all-consuming (“I missed the whole 90s,” its star once joked) but a creative dream. David, the stubborn catastrophiser, and Seinfeld, the breezy optimist, would write episodes face-to-face across a double desk and almost never argue. What began as a cult show beneath the dangling sword of cancellation (“too Jewish” was a common critique) suddenly became a cultural juggernaut in season four as David mastered his two great skills: escalating a slim premise into comic delirium and dovetailing multiple storylines with a satisfying click. For a network sitcom, Seinfeld was radically unsentimental – “No hugging, no learning” was the writers’ credo. “I was shocked that they were letting us do this show,” David admits.

Another curious feature of David’s career is that he didn’t become recognisable until he was in his 50s. Even when he was the showrunner and chief writer of the biggest show on television, with more than 35 million viewers a week, he was effectively unknown. That phase ended in 1998 when the divisively downbeat Seinfeld finale coincided with the abject failure of his first movie, Sour Grapes. For want of a better idea, he decided to return to standup.

Curb Your Enthusiasm began as a one-hour HBO special, framing the routine with a mockumentary, but the frame proved funnier than the picture so Curb turned into a show about “Larry David” at war with the world. Like Seinfeld, it built complex stories out of minute observations and petty grievances but this time there was no script, just an outline to improvise around. “Your job, basically, is to push Larry David into a corner so that he comes bursting out even more Larry,” explains his friend Ted Danson, who played himself. As abrasive as David’s buzzsaw voice, Curb made Seinfeld look like Friends. Its success made David famous as his worst self. “I know people don’t realise it,” says Danson’s wife and Curb co-star Mary Steenburgen, “but Larry really is a sweetheart.”

This is the kind of biography you read for the work rather than the life. Fiercely private and averse to analysis, David doesn’t say much about his divorce in 2007 or Lewis’s death in 2024, nor money (he’s worth an estimated $400m), nor politics (he’s a ferocious Trump-basher). Most of the details about his childhood come from his brother Ken. His only hobby is golf. As Harris notes, David is as much an observer of his own life as a participant, turning everything into material.

So what do we learn about Larry David? He’s a loyal friend, a loving father and a generous comedy partner. His comedy idols are Mel Brooks, Woody Allen and Phil Silvers’ character Sgt Bilko. As seen on Curb, he tends to start laughing when people are upset with him and gets absurdly indignant about minor injustices (though less so since becoming a father in 1994). He bypasses niceties – a “social assassin” in Curb-speak. “He’s comfortable being uncomfortable,” summarises Lewis. “He knows exactly what he wants to do. And he doesn’t need praise.”

Perhaps the key is David’s paradoxical self-esteem. According to Alexander, “At any given moment, he could say, ‘I’m the most worthless, pathetic no-talent in the world,’ and ‘Why is no one giving me my due? I should be doing much better than I’m doing!’ And it was all in the same breath.” Such a person either sinks without trace or, very occasionally, triumphs despite himself.

entries.title: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movement
entries.summary: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin“Everyone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no bus
entries.content:
“Everyone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no business in the Middle East” and Zionism as a “terrible mistake”. Moser, who recently turned 50, admits: “I was not even aware that Zionism was controversial.” The shift in perspective culminated in a visit to the occupied territories in 2016, during which he found “the reality of the occupation of Palestine … deranging”.

His new book includes 12 portraits of Jewish figures who have opposed Zionism, a movement formed in the late 19th century to advocate for the creation of a homeland for Jewish people in Palestine. It is contentious to oppose Zionism today, but Moser wants contemporary Jewish activists to “feel less alone” by showing that debates about Zionism were once mainstream in Jewish communal life. While around 90% of American Jews now support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state (although fewer identify as Zionists), fewer than 1% belonged to the largest American Zionist organisation in 1914. The first character study is of Rabbi Aaron Samuel Tamares, who thought that Judaism offered a vision of a world beyond the devastating nationalism of the first world war. The book closes with a moving account of the photographer Nan Goldin, who spoke out, at considerable cost, as the assault on Gaza began in 2023 following the October 7th attacks.

Many of the protagonists, like Moser, were once committed Zionists. When he was 10, Ronnie Kasrils set up a stall in front of his home in South Africa to sell toys and raise funds for Israel. He was later an anti-apartheid leader who became an ardent anti-Zionist during 27 years living abroad in exile: “Ronnie drives them crazy,” a friend of his tells Moser. “And a lot of it is because he’s so Jewish.”

Jacob Israël de Haan, an influential Dutch poet, wrote in 1912: “We want our own Land, our own Language, our own Art.” He was horrified after he relocated to Mandatory Palestine: “Zionism is a beautiful ideal,” he lamented, but it had “fallen into the hands of hustlers”. He was murdered in 1924 by Avraham Tehomi, a 21-year-old member of the Haganah paramilitary organisation, after his increasingly outspoken opposition to the Zionist leadership.

Hannah Arendt worked for Youth Aliyah in Paris, supporting refugee children to immigrate to Palestine, after fleeing from Germany herself in 1933. Her orientation changed after the Biltmore Conference in 1942, when some 600 delegates from Zionist organisations gathered in New York. Before Biltmore, some in the movement still imagined a single state rooted in the historically strong relations between Jews, Muslims and Christians in Palestine. The Holocaust sharpened the urgency of the argument for a Jewish state instead, but Arendt warned that this would leave the Arabs with “the choice between voluntary emigration or second-class citizenship”. She foresaw, Moser writes, that “a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security”.

Moser’s study includes many instances of despair. The scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjects, many of whom are demonised or accused of antisemitism “so promiscuously that the word would eventually become meaningless”. After the Occupation of Gaza and the West Bank began in 1967, the lawyer Felicia Langer dedicated her life to representing Palestinians. Her first clients, Sheikh Musa al-Bukhari and his wife, knew their son was in prison: “Nobody would tell them why, but when he had picked up his son’s clothes to wash them, he had found a shirt covered with blood.” Langer came to see “the State of Israel as a criminal enterprise” and emigrated in 1990 because she no longer believed it could be reformed.

The Arab-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who was born in Iraq, was at the forefront of revising the established Israeli histories of 1948 and describes being “radicalised in the [Israeli State] archives … I didn’t have any revisionist ideas. It was the material I was reading which completely, flatly contradicted the official line.” Shlaim describes the situation today as “utterly bleak”. In 2023 he argued: “For all its sins, Israel has not engaged in genocide.” In 2025 he published a book called Genocide in Gaza.

Moser’s focus on individual lives is affecting. He makes no claims to be writing a definitive history and is aware of the Palestinian lives that shadow those of his protagonists but fall outside the scope of this study. There are nonetheless gaps. For example, there is no mention of the Satmar Hasidic movement, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish group that believes it is forbidden to establish a Jewish state before the Messiah’s arrival, showing that anti-Zionism can also be theological and conservative.

Early in Anti-Zionism, Moser reads his grandfather’s copy of Theodor Herzl’s founding Zionist text, Der Judenstaat, and finds it “disquieting”, at best a fairytale and at worst a profoundly disturbing vision. Moser wonders how his own life might have been different “if I had grown up with the Palestinian story” instead. This beautifully written cri de coeur is inspired by an “exilic vision” of equality, an alternative Jewish tradition, resistant to nationalism and rooted in solidarity with others.

Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: ‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasy
entries.summary: Critics mock it as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre is much older, and wilder, than you might imagineThere’s a popular genre, filled with beautiful, human-sized fairies having sex with humans (often quite violent sex, but the people reading it seem to enjoy it). entries.content:
There’s a popular genre, filled with beautiful, human-sized fairies having sex with humans (often quite violent sex, but the people reading it seem to enjoy it). Word is that it’s badly written and unashamedly escapist – all golden, glittering palaces, wild adventure and, of course, gorgeous fairies. It’s certainly popular – plenty of the stories have been translated into numerous languages, spreading across continents. Serious commentators are sure it spells bad news: at best, it’s just a load of trash; at worst, it’s actively leading people astray. Most damningly of all, women produce and consume it. Welcome to the 12th century, where fairy romance is all the rage. Sound familiar?

The romantasy that fills our shelves and bestseller lists – from Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses to Callie Hart’s Quicksilver – is not a new genre, but part of a centuries-old heritage. You only need to look at the medieval predecessors of the modern romantasy novel to understand why it’s enjoyed by millions and why, even after hundreds of years, fairy romance has such power over us – and why there are still those who want to diminish and dismiss it.

Medieval romances originated in the French courts of the late 1100s and were wildly popular, quickly spreading throughout Europe, not only from country to country, but also down the social scale, so that even farm workers and impoverished nuns knew the stories. They drew on tales of fairies in earlier myths, especially within Arthurian legends, and were adapted and expanded to be as thrilling as possible, providing people with the same escapism that romantasy does today. Read either the medieval or the modern tales and you’ll find glitter and blood and adventure, not to mention crystal palaces, glorious and perilous enchanted realms, terrifyingly handsome fairy knights, and queens who live in unearthly splendour. As one author of a 13th-century romance pointed out, speaking about the real world brings “grief and torment” – so why not turn to fairies?

The wild sexual freedom of modern romantasy was there in medieval romance too, which overflowed with sexually active fairies, both male and female. There are detailed descriptions of fairy bodies, legs and breasts, and while the veil tends to be drawn over the act itself, both fairies and mortals are always “taking what they desire”, “making merry together”, “holding each other in their arms” and getting each other pregnant – even when either the mortal or fairy is married to someone else, or has only just met. And while there are fairy lovers who are kind, gentle and courteous, medieval audiences also thrilled to the idea of a brooding fairy shadow-daddy: the fairies often simmer with threat, never losing their darker edges even when the story ends with the lovers paired off happily. As with romantasy today, the medieval stories, by dint of being fictional, were a safe place to experiment with sex in a repressed society.

This was even more important as medieval romance, like modern romantasy, was often written by women (such as the 12th-century poet Marie de France), and had a large female audience (something even Chaucer commented on) – so these stories were often a place for women to explore their desires, free from the idea that they should be chaste and subservient. (For reasons too complex to get into it right now, it was generally accepted that fairy sex didn’t quite count, so women who slept with fairies were still thought of as virgins.)

Romantasy still provides this space now: although women may be more sexually liberated than they were in the middle ages, we’re often still uncomfortable with female desires. It’s certainly not a coincidence that many romantasy books today are targeted at teenage girls, who may not be able to talk openly about sex, and are popular with women from more conservative backgrounds. And while the darker, more coercive side of fairy relationships (in both modernity and the middle ages) likely reflects the common fantasy of being overwhelmed, it also helps to alleviate any lingering guilt – after all, the less consensual the encounter, the less the mortal party can be blamed for it.

These stories include a freedom from gender roles as well: in modern romantasy, women are the heroes, the drivers of the plots (the heroine of Saara El-Arifi’s Faebound is an elf military leader; in A Court of Thorns and Roses, a female hunter takes centre stage), while the male love interests, while apparently threatening, are normally intensely loving and vulnerable underneath. Medieval romances also flipped gender roles: you might think it’s a genre of knights rescuing damsels in distress, but more often than not it’s about powerful fairy queens rescuing distressed knights. Take the 12th-century narrative poem Lanval, for example, the story of a penniless and overlooked knight saved multiple times by his beloved fairy queen, that ends with her riding away to fairyland with him behind her on her horse.

While the appeal of all this to the female writers and readers is clear, men happily indulged in these fantasies, too. Lanval was written by a woman but later translated by a man. Even in recent years, it’s been reported that 18% of romantasy readers in the US are men, who enjoy the tales of male characters who love openly and unashamedly, and the strong, powerful women who love them back.

Of course, medieval courts were as familiar with the criticisms of fairy romance as we are. Chaucer even wrote a romance parody – Sir Thopas – about a knight seeking an elf queen. Today, romantasy authors are accused of cheapening popular culture by journalists who often compose articles by flipping through the books looking for the naughty bits, just as Chaucer’s parody featured dirty jokes about elf sex. As a genre, it’s easy to mock, easy to dismiss the stories as “smut” and nothing more.

But this alone can’t explain the ridicule – after all, there are plenty of modern fantasy books crammed with sex that get praised (take George RR Martin’s A Game of Thrones, for example). Instead, the vitriol seems to stem from the fact that it’s a genre enjoyed by women. In the 14th century we had Chaucer mockingly claiming that women held romances “in full great reverence” and clergymen complaining vociferously about the fact that women listen to romances “joyously and willingly”; today the genre is accused of making women stupid, with critics arguing that sexy queens shouldn’t be discussed at literary festivals.

The irony is that fairy romance gave us plenty of great literature, some still well known today (Shakespeare’s Titania and Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream are straight out of romances, while Don Quixote is a romance parody, though heart­breakingly fairy-free); others have been largely forgotten (like one of my absolute favourites, the story of Guingamor). Fairy romance also gave us a huge number of long-forgotten fun romps (my secret heart belongs to the 13th-century Claris and Laris – more than 30,000 lines of pure fairy nonsense).

Medieval romance faded from fashion in the late 1500s, after four glorious, fairy-filled centuries, in part because fairies themselves were changing – becoming miniature, flittering things that were less appealing as lovers (unless you had some fairly niche tastes). But while it is depressing that criticism has not moved on since the middle ages, it’s an utter joy to see female-centred fairy fantasies returning, hundreds of years after the first medieval romances were composed. So why not read some of the medieval romances, along with modern romantasy? You’d be participating in a centuries-old genre of freedom, imagination and joy, and I’m not sure you can ask for more than that.

entries.title: The problem with telling people the world is ending
entries.summary: In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?These days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable.It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The
entries.content:
These days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable.

It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The sense of impending doom, on the other hand, is nothing new. And what we have learned from the past is that doomerism can lead to paralysis. If everyone freezes, then nothing changes – but if we want to have a chance of mitigating some of the threats I’ve mentioned then action is what’s required.

In 1947, The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists created an infamous magazine cover with a “Doomsday Clock”. The hands move closer to midnight whenever events push humanity a little closer to catastrophe. They move back when we make the world a little safer. The original setting was seven minutes to midnight, and the hands are now a mere 85 seconds away.

The Doomsday Clock was a particularly memorable form of crisis communication. The idea was to wake people from their day-to-day routines and help them realise the grave risks facing us. As such, it stands in a long tradition of debate about how to inform, warn and inspire members of the public to take action.

On one end of the spectrum are the doomers. These are often activists and whistleblowers who feel a genuine sense of dread about imminent disaster, and want to inspire the same alarm in others. Recently, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon made headlines by arguing that frontier AI models pose an existential risk to humanity.

At the other end are critics who tend to dismiss these calls as either overblown or self-serving. These folks argue that hyperbolic claims either lead to needless panic or distract from more important issues.

I find myself in a third camp of people who harbour sincere concerns about the problems facing humanity, but worry that feelings of dread will immobilise people. Inaction is a sensible response if you are led to believe that we are past the point of no return, or that the scope of the problem is so immense that anything you do won’t make a difference.

The problem with doomerism isn’t necessarily that the risks are exaggerated, but that it may create a self-fulfilling prophecy – by engendering helplessness, rather than galvanising people.

This aspect of human psychology has been well known for many years by experts on persuasion. When people hear messages designed to appeal to our fears, they can be moved to take action. But this only tends to work as a one-off, and only then when the messages convey a sense of efficacy – a belief that it’s still possible to make a difference. By contrast, if people are inundated with scary and overwhelming stories about the climate or AI, they tune out. Like the boy who cried wolf, those bearing these messages can quickly find themselves ignored.

A big problem for us now, then, is that the modern information ecosystem tends to reinforce negativity. For decades, a core principle in the news business has been “if it bleeds, it leads”. This came from an understanding among journalists that humans are drawn to bad news. This principle now dominates what you see online.

My colleagues and I looked at traffic to news stories on Upworthy.com. This was a website that became famous for conducting A/B tests of headlines to see which one drove clicks, and then using the most popular headline. We analysed 22,743 of these mini-experiments and found that each additional negative word in a headline increased clicks by 2.3%. Psychologists call this the negativity bias: bad is more attention-grabbing than good.

So how does consuming these stories affect our behaviour? We tested the impact of negative messaging around climate in a massive study with 59,440 participants in 63 countries. We had climate experts create 11 different messages to determine exactly which of them changed beliefs and mobilised people to take real action.

The messages included emphasising scientific consensus (for example, noting that “99% of expert climate scientists” agree on the facts), social norms (stating that a majority of people in each nation was concerned), consequences for one’s region (emphasising the increased frequency and severity of wildfires and floods) or the effects of climate change on future generations (asking participants to imagine writing a letter about their actions regarding the climate crisis that would be read by people decades from now).

We also included a text loaded with doom and gloom that told participants: “If your anxiety about climate change is dominated by fears of starving polar bears, glaciers melting and sea levels rising, you are barely scratching the surface of what terrors are possible, even within the lifetime of a young adult today. And yet the swelling seas – and the cities they will drown – have so dominated the picture of climate change/global warming that they have blinded us to other threats, many much closer at hand and much more catastrophic …”

This terrifying passage was the one that proved most effective at getting people to spread it on the internet or social media. But like other fear appeals, it failed in inspiring real action: it was the single worst message for getting people to make the time and effort to mitigate climate effects – by planting trees, for example. It also failed to increase belief in the climate emergency or support for climate policies.

This absolutely doesn’t mean we should avoid sharing the facts about the climate crisis. The message that emphasised the overwhelming scientific consensus noted that the “Earth is warming and climate change is happening” due to human activity. It was more effective than negativity on every outcome we measured, except for sharing on the internet. It conveyed the facts in a sober manner, with the backing of 99% of climate scientists.

What this shows is that, instead of making people feel inept and miserable, we need to take the exact opposite approach. Scientific consensus isn’t the only powerfully motivating message. My PhD student Danielle Goldwert has found that telling people about the potential emotional benefits of climate action – such as increased hope and connection – makes them significantly more likely to take action, be it political participation, advocacy, donating money to climate causes or changing their lifestyle.

If we want to motivate people in the face of dire threats, we must give them a reason to hope. Without that, we are destined to doomscroll while the world burns.

Jay Van Bavel is a professor of psychology and neural science at New York University.

Further reading



Not the End of the World by Hannah Ritchie (Vintage, £18.99

Hope in the Dark by Rebecca Solnit (Canongate, £10.99)

The Future We Choose by Christiana Figueres and Tom Rivett-Carnac (Vintage, £12.99)

entries.title: ‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisis
entries.summary: The author talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novelFor a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers. There
entries.content:
For a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers. There Are Rivers in the Sky, which follows a single raindrop from ancient Nineveh to the River Tigris in 2018, was one of the UK’s bestselling literary novels last year. The Island of Missing Trees, a love story set in post-colonial Cyprus and contemporary London, was shortlisted for the Women’s prize in 2022, and 10 Minutes 38 seconds in This Strange World, narrated by a murdered sex worker in Istanbul, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2019. Last December she was elected president of the Royal Society of Literature. It would be tempting to say she is on a roll, but Shafak’s reputation and readership have been steadily growing for more than 20 years and spanning as many books, of which 14 are novels.

In a 2017 Ted Talk, which has been viewed more than 6.4m times, she describes herself as an Istanbulite, “a European by birth and by choice” and a Londoner for many years. “I like to think of myself as a global soul, as a world citizen, a nomad and an itinerant storyteller.” Her novels sweep confidently across centuries and continents, taking in politics, history, feminism and ecology, typically with a dash of magic realism or mysticism.

Her latest, In One Brief Moment All Eternity, is a stylistically inventive fictionalised life of Gustave Flaubert. “This book is really my love letter to literature,” Shafak says over coffee in west London, where the 54-year-old author has lived with her husband and two children for the past 18 years. While Flaubert is now considered the godfather of the modern novel – as Nabokov said, without Flaubert there would have been no Marcel Proust or James Joyce – most of his life was spent toiling in obscurity. It is this that interests Shafak. “The book is about a lonely boy who was misunderstood by almost everyone around him, including his own family members. He was regarded as a failure, as a disappointment, treated as ‘the other’.” The novel is dedicated to anyone who may have felt similarly treated. “I wanted to be able to say, ‘you’re my brother, you’re my sister’. That was the beginning,” she says.

Shafak talks with the same fluency and lyrical intensity as she writes, in long, far-reaching sentences. In person, she also listens intently and smiles often, despite the seriousness of her words. We last met when she was part of the panel to discuss the Guardian’s 100 best novels of all time list earlier this year: Madame Bovary was in her top 10, but, like Flaubert himself, she is a huge fan of Don Quixote. On stage, she had the softest voice, but when she speaks, everyone listens. She has recently enjoyed renewed popularity with younger readers on BookTok. It is no wonder there are snaking queues of readers of all ages and nationalities for the signings after her literary events.

In One Brief Moment All Eternity arose out of our own historical moment, which Shafak has dubbed “The age of three As: Angst, Anger and AI”. Yet it also started from “a very personal place”, she says, when she was struggling with depression and anxiety, or hüzün in Turkish, meaning a deep melancholy. “In the middle of a world shaped by wars and violence, division, climate crisis, technological uncertainties, you find yourself asking, ‘What is the meaning of shutting yourself in a small room and worrying about the perfect synonym?’” she says. “Is there any value in writing a short story, a poem, a novel in a time of crisis and chaos, such as the one we’re going through? I wanted to take a closer look at this question – creativity in a time of crisis.”

This led her back to the 19th century, another era of change and confusion, in which “there lived a beloved novelist who dedicated his entire life to literature in a very passionate way”. While Flaubert set out to inhabit the female mind – then a radical proposition for a male novelist – Shafak upends the premise of Madame Bovary to tell his story through multiple women whose paths may have crossed with his. “I wanted to bring together the European canon of the novel with the Middle Eastern oral tradition of storytelling,” she explains. “You open a box and inside there’s another box, under this story, there’s another story. There’s a polyphony of voices.”

And so Flaubert’s life is told not just through the eyes of his beloved nursemaid, Julie; his maman; his long-term mistress, Louise Colet; and his confidant George Sand, but also an acrobat he encounters as a boy, a camel called Jamilah and Emma Bovary herself. We meet an Egyptian dancer and courtesan, Kuchuck Hanem, with whom Flaubert becomes enraptured on his travels in the Middle East, passingly mentioned in biographies. “I wanted to remember this woman and say, ‘Maybe this is the woman who inspired Madame Bovary,’” Shafak says. “I want to claim that at the heart of this iconic French European literary heroine, there is an Egyptian belly dancer.” Opium, syphilis and Istanbul (Shafak always thinks of the city as “she”) are also given their own chapters.

“Every time I start writing a book, I say to myself, ‘This time I’m going to keep it minimalist,’” she laughs. “I think because of who I am, my upbringing, all these cultural influences are like tributaries that flow into it. We are all interconnected, not only with each other as fellow human beings, but with nature. For me, the long narrative form is about honouring those connections.”

They may be separated by nearly two centuries, by nationality and by gender, but once she started looking, the connections between Flaubert’s story and her own were striking, “starting with that lonely childhood, with that feeling of being the other,” she says.

Although her parents were Turkish, Shafak was born in Strasbourg, France, in 1971, where her father was studying for a PhD. Her parents divorced five years later and the young Elif and her mother returned to live with her maternal grandmother in Ankara. Like Flaubert, Shafak grew up with two maternal figures. Although her grandmother was uneducated, she insisted her mother return to university, which she had left when she married. Shafak called her mother “big sister”, her grandmother “mother”: “From one I got my love for written culture, from the other I got my love for oral storytelling,” she says. She remembers her grandmother’s flat as a place full of magic, lefty students and Gauloises cigarette smoke.

For all the love in her childhood, Shafak felt abandoned by her father, an academic who remarried. Like the celebrated Doctor Flaubert, Gustave’s father, he was “very detached, very aloof”. She didn’t see him for most of her childhood, and for a long time was very angry that he was such a good father to her half-brothers. “I felt like I was the forgotten child. There was a void. There was an absence of love,” she says. “And I think absences also shape us. Silences also shape us.”

After she finally graduated, her mother became a teacher and then a diplomat. When Shafak was 10, they moved to Madrid, where she was the only Turkish pupil in the international school. As a teenager, she lived in Jordan and Germany. “Throughout all those years when I was really very lonely, books were my friends.” Shafak returned to Ankara to take a degree in international relations, followed by a PhD in political science. In her 20s, after teaching in Istanbul, she “escaped” to study in the US. Her first novel, Pinhan (The Sufi), was met with acclaim when it was published in Turkey in 1997. But her decision to write her fifth novel, The Saint of Incipient Insanities, in English was considered a betrayal by many at home.

The most significant parallel between Flaubert and Shafak is that they have both had their work put on trial: Madame Bovary for obscenity charges in 1857 and Shafak’s The Bastard of Istanbul in 2006, for “the public denigration” of Turkishness, due to her having written about the Armenian genocide. Shafak had to live with a bodyguard for a year and a half. Her picture was burned and spat on. She was acquitted, but in 2019 her novel 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World was investigated by Turkish authorities for “crimes of obscenity” along with two earlier books, The Gaze and Three Daughters of Eve, which dealt with material such as child brides and sexual harassment. Her husband, Eyüp Can, a Turkish journalist and former editor of the Turkish liberal newspaper, Radikal, was put on a wanted list as part of President Erdoğan’s crackdown on intellectuals after the failed coup in Turkey in 2016.

She has described being a writer in Turkey as “a bit like being kissed on one cheek and slapped on the other”, with the kiss from the readers and the slap from the government. She is keen to stress how much her books are loved back home. “In countries like Turkey, a book is not a personal item. If you like a novel, you can’t just put it back on the shelf. You give it to your auntie, the auntie gives it to her neighbour. It’s incredibly heartwarming.”

But she again found herself at the centre of a storm back home after her 2017 Ted talk, titled “The revolutionary power of diverse thought”, in which she came out as bisexual. “I don’t know if it’s brave,” she says now. “I wish I could have done it before. But the abuse that I received from my own motherland for weeks uninterrupted was quite, quite bruising.”

She hasn’t been back to Turkey for 11 years. “There’s a melancholy to it. Maybe I’m in self-imposed exile,” she says. “But as a writer, I need freedom. I need the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speech. I felt like I first migrated into the English language and then into the UK. London became home. And I now feel rooted here, and I say this as someone who has led a very nomadic life.”

Her daughter and son, who have just left home for the new university term, have grown up speaking English. Her elderly mother often stays with them for long periods. “I hope I’m not offending, but I think only a few male authors above a certain age have precise writing schedules,” she says wryly. “Everyone else just juggles multiple roles.” She often writes at night, while listening to heavy metal, melodic death metal in particular, on her headphones. She plays the same song on a loop, often 80 or 90 times. She is a fan of the Armenian-American band System of a Down, who have also been very vocal about the Armenian genocide. “I love it. It gives me such energy,” she says. And somehow this makes her fiction “calmer”.

But it doesn’t make her calm. Writing doesn’t come any easier as you get older, she says. “It doesn’t matter whether it’s your first book, fifth book, tenth book, you suffer. You sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt. There’s a lot of anxiety, panic attacks. That, too, is part of the creative process.” When she is finished, she is not filled with satisfaction or pride, but grief. “I feel a sense of loss,” she says. “I find it so difficult to let go of the characters.”

Then she goes back out into the world. She thinks it is really important for women to have a voice in public life, and surprises herself by how much she loves literary festivals. “I really am an introvert by nature, so my natural habitat is just a small room full of books,” she says. “But when I’m on stage doing a literary event, it is not a chore. It’s not a burden. It is an immense treat for the mind or the soul.” As someone for whom speaking out has led to threats of imprisonment, she is frustrated by the cynicism towards intellectualism in the UK and the US. “It’s regarded as a sign of arrogance, hubris,” she says. “I’m not claiming to be an intellectual. What I am claiming is I have a lot of respect for the intellect.”

For Shafak, literature is “one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we’re not rushing from one thing to the next, we’re not just being fed snippets of information, but we slow down and we listen to each other again,” she says. “The ancient art of storytelling is so universal. It’s so timeless. It really doesn’t belong to a single ethnicity, region or religion. It belongs to all humanity. When I’m writing and in my books, I try to remember that kind of … ” For a moment she is lost for words. “I don’t know what to call it other than shared humanity.”

entries.title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym
entries.summary: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the SpiritsThe Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with
entries.content:
The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.

“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.

“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”

The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

entries.title: The best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis Spufford
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection. Discuss what you’re reading in paperback in the comments*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Shadow Ticket

Thomas Pynchon

Everything is connected in Shadow Ticket, Thomas Pynchon’s fleet-footed noir fiction about a lindy-hopping detective in prohibition-era Wisconsin. The homemade bomb connects to the runaway cheese heiress, the cheese heiress to the federal agents, and the feds to the pro‑Nazi leagues at the bowling lanes outside town. Early-30s Milwaukee, in turn, is connected to powder-keg central Europe, where paramilitary groups have pitched camp on the Hungaro-Croatian border and guest speakers wax lyrical about “our immense fascist future”. Most likely it connects to the current moment as well, albeit wryly and slyly, with a nonchalant swing. That’s the implied final move of this merry dance of a book: the point where the past links its hands with the present.

Shadow Ticket is a Pynchon novel – the 88-year-old’s first in 12 years; his ninth overall – and so it naturally connects to the man’s back catalogue, too, and its abiding fascination with conspiracy, chaos and the churn of American pop culture. Specifically it relates back to his two previous works – Inherent Vice and Bleeding Edge – in that the story comes tailored as a dime-store whodunnit, complete with red herrings, plot twists and reams of hard-boiled dialogue. But classifications, like people, are never entirely to be trusted. Pynchon inhabits the genre like a hermit crab inside a mollusc shell, periodically peeking out from the gloom to remind us that he’s there. Xan Brooks

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Nonesuch

Francis Spufford

Spufford’s fourth work of fiction in a genre-spanning oeuvre, Nonesuch is a historical fantasy set during the second world war, every paragraph of which is packed with authorial zest. The novel opens in London, August 1939: war has been declared, but hasn’t yet made its reality felt in the city’s streets, and Iris Hawkins, an ambitious office clerk, makes her way through the sun-baked West End in a slinky dress. One half of a disastrous date later, she’s being whisked away to a DIY surrealist film club in bohemian Bloomsbury – not her scene at all – and two extremely fateful introductions: the first to Geoffrey Hale, a sweetly apprehensive BBC television engineer; and the second to the object of Geoffrey’s guileless infatuation, one Lady Lalage Cunningham, an icy aristocratic beauty with amazing hair and worrisome political sympathies. Cue chaos. Nonesuch follows the bolshy Iris from her seedy summer’s night through a regrettable Hampstead hook-up, and, eventually, neck-deep into a time-travelling plot by “magical fascist lunatics” to assassinate Winston Churchill. The novel is a pleasing pasticcio of romance, occultism, non-Euclidean geometry and airborne adventure across the blitz-stricken rooftops of London. It is difficult to imagine it would hold together quite so well in other hands than Spufford’s. AK Blakemore

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Beasts of the Sea

Iida Turpeinen



In November 1741 Georg Wilhelm Steller, “theologian, naturalist, and curious man”, was shipwrecked on an island between Alaska and Russia. There he found, floating in the shallow waters, a vast sirenian, Hydrodamalis gigas, nine feet long and soon to be known as Steller’s sea cow. Having made it through the winter, largely by eating the sea cows, the following August Steller and the remaining survivors of the Great Northern Expedition left the island. Within 30 years, Steller’s sea cow was hunted to extinction.

Having described these events, Finnish author Iida Turpeinen’s debut novel goes on to describe the lives of other historical figures, each of whom are touched in some way by the sea cow, now reduced to bones. There is Hampus Furuhjelm, governor of Alaska, in search of a complete skeleton, and his sister Constance, who finds peace and intellectual autonomy among her taxidermy collection. Later, there’s Hilda Olson, a scientific illustrator, and John Grönvall, specialist in the reconstruction of birds’ eggs, who is tasked with preparing a sea cow’s relics for exhibition.

Turpeinen writes in a flowing present tense, moving seamlessly from one character to another, drawing us gently but firmly onwards. Emotional detail is astutely rendered. The result is a book that is almost hypnotically readable; it’s been much garlanded in Finland and it’s easy to see why. Jessie Greengrass

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Other People’s Fun

Harriet Lane

Ruth, the narrator of Harriet Lane’s third novel, Other People’s Fun, is corroded by envy. Alone, her marriage over, her daughter grown and her freelance work as dull as it is low paid, she is that most dangerous of characters: an overlooked middle-aged woman with nothing to lose. When she bumps into beautiful, stupid and entitled Sookie at a school reunion, she reconnects with her teenage self “and all her violent desires”. Having flown under the radar as a pupil, noticed by Sookie only because she lent her her essays, she has perfect recall of her own petty humiliations, now amplified by the fact that she can stalk her contemporaries’ “best lives” on social media, while almost none of them remember her.

The best comedy is sharpened by pain, and what Lane has pinpointed in her flint-sharp novel is something that has a highly modern resonance as the world of the haves and have-nots becomes increasingly polarised and toxic. When Ruth gets her revenge, it is as nasty as it is total. You will, I fear, howl with satisfaction. Amanda Craig

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Absence

Issa Quincy

In Quincy’s novel, the narrator is charmed by a poem first read to him as a child by his mother, which then follows him through his life. He’s stirred by memories and emotions as he is confronted by letters and photographs, phantoms and secrets, all of which make up a life that has been affected by generations of profound familial tragedy. Quincy’s prose is deftly lyrical and imaginative; I’ve had the pleasure of hearing him read from Absence at a literary salon in London and it was entrancing. He observes the fragility of memory, and what remains after our encounters, however fleeting, with people, say a schoolteacher or an estranged aunt; you might think of him as a counterpart to the novelists Rachel Cusk and Teju Cole. Jason Okundaye

  • Absence is published by Granta

Short stories

Short stories

The Land of Sweet Forever

Harper Lee

The Land of Sweet Forever is a collection of Lee’s unpublished short stories and previously uncollected essays. However, like most such books, it has little to offer to those who aren’t diehard fans.

The short stories, written in Lee’s youth, are all badly underdeveloped. Most fail to work even as vignettes. One centres on trying to find a place to unload a truck in Manhattan; another on a temporary change to the way the doxology is sung in a Methodist church. A slender piece about the quirks of New York movie audiences is categorised as a story, but feels more like a newspaper sketch. The young Lee seems to have little sense of what a story is.

On the positive side, there is already wit and charisma in the voice. One narrator, returning to her southern home town, recognises “a tall young man whose face belonged to the Wade family, but whose body showed extensive Talbert influence. He was Talbert Wade, of course.” This may be slight, but it’s elegantly done. There are also hints of iconoclastic anger struggling to get out, especially in The Water Tower, where a 12-year-old Mississippi girl erroneously thinks she is pregnant. Understanding that being an unwed mother would wreck the lives of her whole family, she decides the only way to save them is to destroy her shameful body.

If we regard this book as literature, it is an unqualified failure. But it’s more properly seen – and will surely be read – for the light it sheds on Lee’s life. As such, it’s obliquely fascinating, largely because it radiates repression. Often there’s a sense that we’re seeing the side of Harper Lee that wasn’t exceptional, but representative of a generation of women who were mostly muzzled. Lee writes in The Cat’s Meow (perhaps the strongest story in the collection): “I suppose a lot of people like me have mastered the first lesson of living at home these days: if you don’t agree with what you hear, place your tongue between your teeth and bite hard.” We feel those painfully gritted teeth on every page of this book. In a time of rising censorship, it’s salutary to be reminded that an author as important as Harper Lee came so close to being entirely silenced. Sandra Newman

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Essays

Essays

Dead and Alive

Zadie Smith

Dead and Alive bundles various odds and ends from the past nine years: speeches, opinion pieces, criticism and eulogies for departed literary heroes – Philip Roth, Martin Amis, Hilary Mantel.

In Some Notes on Mediated Time – one of three completely new essays in the collection – Smith recalls how the “dreamy, slo-mo world” of her 1980s childhood gave way, within a generation, to the “anxious, permanent now” of social media. If you lived through that transition, you don’t have to be very old to feel ancient. When this estrangement is compounded by the ordinary anxieties of ageing, cultural commentary becomes inflected with self-pity. Smith’s identification with the protagonist of Todd Field’s Tár, a once revered conductor who finds herself shunned by the younger cohort, takes on existential proportions: “Our backs hurt, the kids don’t like Bach any more – and the seas are rising!”

Smith steers a sensible middle course on the vexed debate around “cultural appropriation” in fiction. There is more to people than their identity – “we can, sometimes, forget the mystery that lies at the heart of all selfhood”. The point is well made in a thoughtful piece on James Baldwin and the craft of writing, originally a lecture delivered to creative writing students over Zoom during the pandemic. Smith reminds her students that the essence of Baldwin’s brilliance was his ability to process politics through personal experience: he “submitted to his consciousness first and then re-examined what that might mean for his conscience”. This is sound advice, and Smith’s positions on the politics of creativity are beyond reproach, albeit commonsensical – amounting, essentially, to a caution against overcorrection and incuriosity.

When it comes to actual politics, she is less assured. Her New Yorker op-ed on the war in Gaza, published in May 2024, was widely interpreted as unhelpfully equivocal, and seemed to conflate anti-war protesters with antisemites. She has since added her signature to an open letter acknowledging Israel’s actions as genocidal. The New Yorker piece, reprinted here with a new preamble hailing the protesters as “heroic”, is an intriguing artefact: the prose is mealy mouthed, heavy on the passive voice – all the more conspicuous since Smith’s writing is normally so clear and crisp. Houman Barekat

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

Fly, Wild Swans

Jung Chang



Remarkable success notoriously brings its own problems. Wild Swans, first published in 1991 and written by Jung Chang with the help of her husband, Irish-born historian and writer Jon Halliday, had a global impact few authors dare to dream of. It told the story of three generations of women in 20th-century China – Chang’s grandmother, her mother and herself – and became one of the most popular nonfiction books in history, selling more than 13m copies in 37 languages and collecting a fistful of awards and commendations. For any author, following that would be a challenge. Now, Fly, Wild Swans returns to the story, picking it up after Chang’s own departure from China in 1978, and revisiting episodes from the earlier work with added detail.

Few can match Chang’s ability to bring Chinese history and politics to life through deeply felt personal narrative, and few have shaped western understanding of China as broadly. Nearly 35 years on from the book that made her name, this story of suffering and success has the air of a closing chapter, a reckoning with both her achievements and the cost of the path she chose. Isabel Hilton

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Wings

Paul McCartney

After splitting up, The Beatles faced an unprecedented challenge: how to be an ex-Beatle? McCartney yearned to play before audiences again, which he hadn’t since the Beatles stopped touring in 1966. But he couldn’t face doing it solo, the spotlight trained on him alone. So he asked Linda to help him put together a new group. This authorised, illustrated oral history, edited by cultural historian Ted Widmer, tells the story of one of the most successful bands of the 1970s – and one of the strangest.

It’s based on interviews (given for a new documentary on the band) with McCartney and former band members, as well as archive material. Widmer does an expert job of stitching this into a compelling narrative that includes cultural context – like what else was in the charts at the time – and plenty of photographs, many previously unseen. The result is a portal into a more eccentric age of pop, a fable about the tension between celebrity and creativity, and a story with elements of Spinal Tap and Wacky Races. Ian Leslie

£19.80 (RRP £22) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop
